Why Companies Fail and How to Build a Profitable Company

Why do companies fail? So companies fail for two main reasons — really, families of reasons. These aren't isolated causes.

One, as I mentioned earlier, this is simply a profession that has nowhere to be learned, and then the CEO shows up and essentially has to reinvent the wheel. That's very expensive, it doesn't work well, so we want to save that time. It's not for nothing that I used the example of a residency in a hospital. Everyone understands that a doctor who completed six years and graduated with honors is still not a doctor. After that, he needs to do a residency, and his specialization is usually in a very narrow sub-field. So you understand the process. Except for the CEO who says "let's go," he's a graduate of 8200, he's got some fantastic algorithm, he'll surely know how to sell and will make the company big. That's not true. It's simply not true.

The second reason is that there's essentially no methodology for how to build companies. And not only is there no methodology, there are many pervasive — what I call wrong assumptions — we'll talk about one of them today — that simply take companies in directions that aren't exactly productive and greatly reduce their chances of success. So we address that and of course we provide guidance and tools on how to actually build things correctly, and I hope that today you'll already see one example and gradually understand how we work here.

To trace back where these pervasive assumptions come from, you need to understand the ecosystem of those who provide the money, because at the end of the day, whoever has the money calls the shots, as we always know. So when someone comes along and is willing to give you several million dollars, they have very, very clear expectations, and rightfully so — it's their money. So let's see what they need.

First of all, what is a VC? A VC doesn't actually use their own money. They raise money from pension funds, insurance companies, places that have enormous amounts of cash, and they take a small portion of it and say "let's put it in venture capital." Then the general partner of that is what we call the venture fund, but it's really just the managers — it's not their money — and they invest in startup companies and in the end they need to return the money to those companies. Meaning, there's a whole cycle here: I gave you money, give me money back. Don't give me shares in a company — I have no use for that. I'm an insurance company, I'm a pension fund. What am I going to do with shares? And therefore the money needs to come back, and for it to come back there must be an exit.

Now, the timelines — that's the interesting thing here. They raise the money, usually in layers, as it's called, and each layer has seven plus three extensions — seven years, and they can get an extension three times — a total of ten years, by which point they must return the money.

What happens sometimes when a VC is stuck at the end with three, four, five companies in their portfolio? There are VC firms that buy their portfolio — they look at the whole package and say, okay, you have these companies, I'll give you fifty million dollars, give me all of those companies.

They invest mainly in the early years so there's time for the company to develop. After that, they continue investing in companies because companies often raise multiple rounds — A, B, C, D, E, probably goes all the way to Z — and the first question every new investor asks is: are you investing in the same company? Because if you're not investing in this company, what happened? Why aren't you investing in it? So that's why they always keep two-thirds of the money for future investments in those same companies, and here the seven years run out and then they want to start doing all the exits. That's how it works, and it creates enormous time pressure on the company.

Usually an exit happens in one of two ways — either an IPO or M&A. M&A is very common. M&A means someone buys you, and there are three types of M&A. The first type is strategic. Meaning, a company is willing to buy you for much more than your economic value. Why are they willing to pay much more than the economic value? Mainly because they say: if I had this product and I have a hundred thousand customers, I could take this product that you haven't sold a single unit of and sell a hundred thousand units, and therefore it's worth a lot of money to me.

Or I need to be in the AI space — I'm a big company like Google — so I'll go and buy DeepMind in London or something like that. I need to be in this space. The fastest way for me to get there is to buy another company. I'm willing to pay astronomical sums. It happens a lot, as we see in the cyber security space.

Financial means I'm buying the company because it's worth money. It generates a million dollars — multiply that by twenty. Why twenty? Because in a bank the most you'll get is four percent; I'll give you roughly five percent times twenty. So a million dollars in profit is as if I put twenty million dollars in the bank, right? If the company is growing, the multiple will be even higher.

And distress. About two-thirds of acquisition announcements — the press release talks about strategic synergy and all sorts of nice things. The only thing missing from the press release is how much money was paid. Usually, when it doesn't say how much was paid, I assume it probably wasn't too great a success. We don't know, but two-thirds of press releases about acquisitions don't contain a number.

Now, how do I increase the chances of a strategic exit? Usually I need unique things — for example, Disruptive Technology like I mentioned earlier: AI, quantum computing, Cyber Security, various Deep Tech things or things of that nature — that's one thing. Or being first to market with something another company wants. Or going after a very, very large market. You say: look, listen, I have something that can fit a big market. I'm a small company; I only addressed a small part of the market. A big company would know how to use it for everyone.

And very fast sales growth. Look, if I'm making enough money I can grow incredibly fast. You have more money — buy me, grow even faster. These are all the stories you hear. I didn't put them here for no reason, because I talked about pervasive beliefs that you hold. You'll hear this from every VC — they want you to be in one of these four, preferably all of them — and we'll try to show you that this isn't necessarily reality, and in many, many cases it leads to not-so-great outcomes.

Why do I say this is a rare event? Because you really need some specific buyer for whom this represents a strategic asset, and you need to be in the right place at the right time at that exact moment. And therefore, in many, many cases it doesn't happen. And then when a company wants to do something amazing, it spends a lot of money, and if there's no potential buyer at that moment, nine out of ten companies disappear.

So let's see what the big players say. I'm bringing you a video clip that some of you have probably already seen, and I think it captures the problem perfectly.

[Clip from the series Silicon Valley]
— Right, Richard, one potential issue: hosting fees can become a challenge as we scale.
— Right, but we can offset a lot of that once we get a few customers and start a subscription revenue model.
— What? Revenue? No, no, no, no revenue. Why would you go after revenue?
— Because to make money.
— No. If you show revenue, people will ask how much, and it will never be enough. The company that was the hundred X or the thousand X becomes the two X dog. But if you have no revenue, you can say you're pre-revenue. You're a potential pure player. It's not about how much you earn, it's about what you're worth and who's worth the most. Companies that lose money — Pinterest, Snapchat, no revenue. Amazon has lost money every quarter for the last twenty years, and Bezos is the king. There's no revenue. No one wants to see revenue, go.
— I just thought that mainly the goal of companies is to make money.
— Yeah, no, that's not how it works. I don't want to make a little bit of money every day. I want to make a fortune all at once.
— ROI.
— ROI. You know what that stands for? Radio on internet.

Now, because the dialogue was very important, I went to the trouble of putting it here as well. What does he say? "We want to make money." And he says: "No, if you show revenue, people will ask how much, and it will never be enough." You get the point? It will never be enough. Why? "The company that was worth a hundred X or a thousand X unicorn" — the kind running around the streets — "becomes the two X dog. But if you have no revenue, you can say you are pre-revenue. You are a potential pure play. It's not about how much you earn, it's about what you are worth and who is worth it for."

I found a clip that describes exactly what the VCs expect from you. They just forgot to mention that nine out of ten disappear and that's probably you. The ten that remain — everyone else already lost. But hey, it was worth being in the front row.

He says: "I thought that the main goal of companies is to make money." He says: "No, no, that's not how it works. I don't want to make a little bit of money every day." I won't repeat all the other words he said. We recommend doing what the CEO says: the purpose of a company is to make money. But I thought it would be very interesting to see someone else saying it. So we got it — we want to be a successful company.

What do we need to do? In order to be a successful company, we need to change the perception of what the company's goal is. From "I must reach an exit" to "I must be a profitable company and the exit will come after that." If I'm lucky and it comes before that, great. Nobody's arguing. But if you first make sure you're a profitable company, something amazing happens. You're alive.

Before an exit happens, it helps to still exist, because if you don't exist, the exit skips right over you. So first of all, in order to succeed in life, it helps to be alive. I know that sounds ridiculous, but when nine out of ten fail, it's not ridiculous at all. If a contractor built ten buildings and nine of them collapsed, he'd be somewhere between prison and fleeing the country. What is this?

What is profitability? Generating money. Month after month after month. I can tell you from experience that when you look at your bank account and you see it growing every month, there's this kind of pleasant feeling. It's a kind of joy — watching your bank account swell every month. It also gives you the feeling that you can do things because you can fund yourself. Like I once asked — why don't we live with our parents? Because part of growing up is supporting ourselves, being able to fund the things we need. The question is how you generate money, and that's going to be our topic of discussion today.

I always try to bring things down to a very basic, almost absurd level. Why? Because it makes you think again. Hold on — forget all the fancy words you learn at university. Life is very simple. How do you make money? You simply bring in more revenue than expenses. Now, when you do it the other way around, you're in overdraft at the bank. That's an expression everyone knows, so it's really advisable to spend less than your salary. It's really advisable that in your company you spend less money than the company brings in.

To understand how to do that, let's start from the expenses side, actually, because that's the simpler side. So typically most companies start on the product development side. Two founders want to develop a product. How many people do they hire to develop the product? Usually you end up with about six people. There are two co-founders — almost always co-founders come in pairs or threes. They bring on two more engineers, whether internal or external, a Product Manager, and a QA Engineer. That's pretty much the basic team.

I try to always bring everything down to the numbers in the end. Why? Because ultimately profit and loss is just numbers. If you earn thirty thousand shekels a month, pay twenty thousand in income tax, you're left with ten thousand. Rent is eleven thousand — you don't eat. That's it. Numbers. But you need to understand the numbers.

You raised a million dollars. You're incredibly talented people, you have a million dollars in the bank. How long will you survive if you have no revenue? Let's say each of your smart people earns thirty thousand shekels per month. Add employer costs on top of that — that's say thirty-nine thousand shekels. Salaries typically represent roughly seventy-five percent of expenses, so that already comes to fifty-two thousand shekels. I used an exchange rate of three point three. Roughly speaking, you're approaching two hundred thousand dollars per employee, which is pretty standard. That's the cost in high-tech companies — around two hundred thousand dollars per employee.

So how long will I survive? If you're alone, you'll survive five point three years, or sixty-three months — my warmest congratulations, may you live long and prosper. With fourteen people, you're probably no longer around. But let's say you're six people — you have eleven months of life. You raised a million dollars, which is a pretty respectable sum, and you have eleven months of life. That means roughly six months or three months after you raised the money, you're in a race to raise the next round. By the way, that's what CEOs spend most of their time doing — running from round to round.

Why give salaries like the ones we're used to in established high-tech and not start with slightly more modest salaries? That's an excellent question. Everything I'm saying is averages, and nobody is average, as we remember, but in averages, that's the average. What happens is of course this: when times are bad, you can play around and give lower salaries. When times are good, you can't get people, and then you raise salaries. Once you give a high salary, you can't lower it. People who get their salary cut don't continue working at the same company. So what happens is that salaries only go up.

Equity is nice, but it doesn't hold up for very long, because at some point the daughter wants to buy a bicycle and the guy wants something else. In short, in the end people want money. I'm not trying to be stingy here. You want something more interesting — not how to penny-pinch to the very end, but how we get to a profitable company.

Now we're going to move to the profitability side. We want to be profitable. We're spending roughly a hundred thousand dollars every month. The question is how do I now generate a hundred thousand dollars in revenue. To be profitable, you need revenue of at least a hundred thousand dollars per month. So let's see how you generate that revenue, and for that purpose I've brought you another video. Because today I have to be entertaining.

[Clip from the movie Field of Dreams]
— If you build it, he will come... People will come, Ray. They'll arrive at your door as innocent as children. It's only twenty dollars per person. They'll pass over the money without even thinking about it.
— I have just created something totally illogical.
— It's a good baseball field, Ray. People will come, Ray.
— Am I completely nuts?
— Sometimes when you believe the impossible, the incredible comes true.

So let me tell you the story. It's about someone who has a dream. He's obsessed with baseball, and he dreams that if he builds a baseball field in the middle of nowhere, in the heart of America, in the cornfields, then those players will rise from the grave and come play at his field and it'll all be genius. So that's the story.

Why did I show you this clip? Because from my experience with a lot of entrepreneurs and companies — it doesn't happen. At the end of the day, somewhere along the way: if you believe the impossible, the incredible will happen. Meaning, I build the most amazing thing on earth. Who wouldn't buy it? Have you seen anyone who wouldn't buy what I built with the sweat of my brow? It's incredible. It's a work of art. It's fantastic. Everyone will buy it. The probability of that happening is roughly in the field of dreams. So it was important to me that you see and understand — it happens, but not often. At these odds, you're better off buying a lottery ticket every week. Every week someone wins the lottery, so the odds are actually better than this.

So what do you do so you don't have to build a field of dreams? Let's go back to how many sales we need to be profitable. We said we raised a million dollars. We're spending ninety-five thousand dollars a month — I rounded it to a hundred. Let's think for a moment about what happens depending on how much I charge for the product: one thousand dollars, two thousand, three thousand, four thousand, and five thousand. How many do I need to sell each month? If the price is a thousand dollars, I need to sell a hundred units per month. I took twenty working days in a month. I'm selling all the time. Every two hours or every hour and something I have to close another thousand-dollar deal. How many people here manage to close a thousand-dollar deal every hour and a half? Field of dreams, guys. If you charge two thousand dollars, you only need half of that — two and a half deals per day.

Why am I showing you this table? Because to reach profitability, you need to confront the question — not how I sold to my neighbor's cousin, and not that someone introduced me to this CEO and he agreed to meet with me. You need to build a mechanism that is scalable and efficient. Meaning, a mechanism that can generate a thousand sales, five hundred sales, constantly — because otherwise you won't reach profitability.

I said the three parameters — profitable, growing fast, and with little money — need to go together. Broadly speaking, this is the main thing I want to talk about here. How do you build an efficient sales mechanism that can take you to profitability? Without it, you won't be profitable. Plain and simple.

So let's start first with the marketing problem. What is marketing? My answer is a bit unusual. Marketing is about wanting to change behavior. Why? Because until you did something, the person didn't buy your product, and now you want them to reach into their pocket and buy your product. They need to change their behavior. If you spent millions of dollars on advertising and not a single person responded, you did nothing in marketing. You need a response. A change in behavior.

Changing behavior takes a long time. Other people's behavior, and especially if you want to change the behavior of a large audience. Think for a moment about Pepsi versus Coca-Cola. They need it so that when I walk into the supermarket and go to grab a can of Coke, I stop and say: no, this time I'll buy Pepsi. Do you know how much effort it takes to get people not to grab the Coke but to grab the Pepsi instead? It's complicated. It takes time and time and time. It's not for nothing that I described earlier how everything translates into time, which translates into money.

The biggest competitor for all of you is doing nothing. Most of us don't like change. There's the electricity reform going on right now. How many of you have already switched under the electricity reform? About thirty to forty percent. Why? I look at myself. I keep getting phone calls. "We can save you seven percent." What does it involve? Nothing. Just sign. And I haven't done it. I have absolutely no idea why I'm not doing it, but I'm not. That's the fact. Just to show you how much people don't like change, including me.

Even a small change is still a change. Think for a moment about what you're doing. All of you are coming with something that's very different. Before it was manual, now you'll have a machine that does it. Autonomous cars — have you ever tried driving an autonomous car? No. Why? Because people don't like change. Don't move my cheese. I'm trying to explain to you the forces working against you, which are much bigger than you think and they're irrational. It's not about logic — it's about human nature, and at the end of the day you need that customer's money. You need to somehow convince them to deviate from their habits, reach into their pocket, and give you money. Not easy.

Now, how do markets behave? There's a very famous book, I think it came out about forty years ago, called Crossing the Chasm by Jeff Moore. What does it describe? It describes market behavior. In the beginning, there's what he defines as the Tech Enthusiast. Meaning, people who will buy every new computer or every new feature. They're the ones standing at midnight outside the Apple store to buy the iPhone. Those are the crazies. They'll always buy, but that's not a market. It's a very, very small part of the market.

After them come the Visionaries. These are people who aren't crazy, but they're willing to be the first to try something, and that's around twelve percent. In total, you have about fifteen percent of the market here. His book argues that the transition from the Visionaries to the Pragmatists — what he calls the Early Majority — is very complicated. It's called the valley of death. But notice how long this whole thing takes. And by the way, this part of the market is very profitable. You know why? Because these people want something that's already established in the market.

There was a product called Word Perfect. Word Perfect was very, very common among law firms. All their documents were in Word Perfect, and then Microsoft Word came along and slowly took over the market. But they were used to Word Perfect. So someone bought the Word Perfect company and raised the price threefold and became very wealthy, because those people would keep buying Word Perfect, because their mental cost of switching to another product was too high. There are many stories showing that this market segment is the most profitable there is, because these customers are captive customers. They'll do anything to stay with the existing product.

Let's start understanding how the sales process works. It's called a Funnel. Someone who has never heard of you enters from the top. What do they need to go through before they buy? First, they need awareness. They need to somehow suddenly realize that something exists. And then you want to get them to a state where they're willing to give their name, fill out some form, or pick up the phone — where they're willing to talk to you. That's called Lead Capture. And then they become a Prospect, and then you get MQLs — Marketing Qualified Leads — and Sales Qualified Leads.

Those of you who have been in marketing or sales know that if we're talking about the valley of death, it sits right here. Why the valley of death? The marketing people say "we did our job." The sales people say "you did nothing," and they fight to the point where they kill each other. Literally the valley of death.

Now let's look at the Marketing Funnel, the very top part. Look at how many activities you can do: blog posts, social media posts, landing pages, ads, social media, and so on. Generally, common wisdom says you need six touch points. Meaning, you have to reach a person at least six times before they even do anything. Remember, you want a change in behavior. That's marketing.

If I asked you what ads you saw while you were on the internet, none of you would remember a single one. Because it's noise. It's constantly appearing there. You drive down the highway, there are billboards, you don't see them at all. We're built to filter out that noise. Breaking through the noise barrier is not easy. And after that, when you finally get to the point where you're talking to a customer, it's complicated to get through that cycle and get people to eventually give you money. In short, we're talking about long and complicated processes, and therefore expensive ones.

Let's take a few examples. This is our company, Pitch Video, and what they do is take a video you've already produced — forty to fifty minutes — and turn it into something that can generate money. What's the product? Not relevant. You have a video, I can show you how to use it better. That's it.

Now the question is who do I sell it to. When you start thinking about it, you discover that there are many market segments that are quite different from each other. I can go to B2B companies — they do webinars, they have round tables, testimonials, they produce a lot of videos. What do they do with those videos? Put them on YouTube, like everyone. When you look at how many people watched the video, something in the range of twenty to seventy views, and of those, probably only two actually watched it. B2C companies too — they have testimonials, user stories. Media companies produce videos in infinite quantities. Event and Conference Organizers, Training companies, influencers, and so on. Each one of them speaks a different language. Each one of them sees the value of this differently.

And that's the key point here. When you go to decide which market to sell to, you have no idea in advance which market will respond to you and to which messages they'll respond. At the beginning of your journey, you worked on the product. Fourteen people. You already built the product. You raised a million dollars, you have a product. Who do I sell it to? There are tons of people, each of them requires a slightly different message, but that's not even everything. These aren't people at all. These are companies.

So who are the people inside the company that I'm trying to go after? There's the Chief Marketing Officer, VP Marketing, Director, Social Media Manager, CEO if it's a small company — anyone who has a title with "video" in it, you name it. And I always put "other" because you almost always discover something you didn't think of. I have tons of types of companies and tons of people I want to reach, and I have absolutely no idea who will respond and to which message they'll respond, and I need to solve all of this.

But that's not the end. What can I do? There are tons of things: Email campaigns, Google AdWords, LinkedIn, Facebook, TikTok, Instagram. There's Retargeting ads, Webinars. In short, there are tons of ways to reach the market. Which one is effective? For which target audience? You don't know. Meaning, we're in an area where there are equations with a million unknowns, because we don't know their solutions. That's reality.

And then of course there's the question of pricing. How do I build my pricing model? What do I charge based on? Do I charge per clip? Based on video quantity? Each minute costs this much? Per gigabyte? In every industry there's a different method for setting prices. Sometimes it's per Seats, sometimes it's per Usage, sometimes it's per Memory. There's no way to know. And of course, what's the actual price itself. So look at how many unknowns exist in order to take this single product that you invested so much work into and bring it to market and make sure someone buys it — and you need it to be Scalable.

Let's take another one of our companies, IntelliChain. What do they do? Demand planning and inventory optimization. Who are we going to sell it to? Same story all over again. In this case, the company is already selling, so I can tell you we had surprises. We planned to go after manufacturing companies, because they have a production line and it's very important for them to forecast — what am I going to sell next month, because I need to produce it. But even this market is very fragmented. There's Perishable — I can't hold the finished product for more than a week, it's cheese or milk. Or Non-Perishable, where I can put it in a warehouse. That's different company behavior.

But we suddenly discovered that importers and distributors also really need this. Why? Because for them, almost all their money is sitting on the shelves. They don't have a production line, so all their money is sitting on the shelves. They have more flexibility, and therefore they're extremely interested in managing this at an optimal level. And then we discovered there's also Spare parts inventory. We work with a company called Chemicals for Israel, a fairly large one. They don't need us to think about which chemicals to produce, but they do need us to think about which spare parts they should keep on hand to make sure that if there's a malfunction, they can fix it immediately.

And how do they actually decide which parts to keep? Based on two parameters: how much the part costs and what damage will be caused if I don't have the part. And suddenly, instead of talking about sales, you're talking about damage. It's the same product, by the way. I'm now telling them: guys, for the spare parts segment, I'm asking you to change what's written in the product — it should say "damage," not "benefit." Why? Because that's what the customer wants to see. All I'm trying to explain here is how incredibly complicated the sales process, the marketing process, and the Packaging process really are. It's not field of dreams.

Let's go back again to the question of "how do you build a Scalable and efficient sales process." To do that, you need to answer a lot of questions: which Segment do we want, what type of advertising, where, what works, what doesn't work, Length of a sale cycle. There are a million questions that need to be answered. The only way to answer these questions is to consult with me — but that doesn't help. And after consulting with me, you simply do trial and error an infinite number of times, and in every good company, this is a process that continues for the entire life of the company. They're constantly improving.

And you do it through trial and error, because at the end of the day, the other side — you always need to remember this — your customers are people. People are complicated. None of you here looks like the person sitting next to you or behaves like the person sitting next to you. Every person is a unique creation and you need to get money out of them, and that's not easy. Second, you want to build a process where you have measurements all the time, because to make Incremental Improvement you must constantly measure what you're doing. In short, it's a long process, and because it's long, it's expensive.

Almost every company I know starts the same way: "I have a genius idea. I thought about it. I know this from my work. I prepare a presentation and I go raise money." In the presentation, there's a huge market. I'm going to change the world, and my sales will look like this — what's called a Hockey Stick. In the beginning, it's slow, but very quickly it shoots through the roof. And then you go raise money, you raised some money, and what do you do? You set up a development team. By the time you've finished developing the product, or you have enough of a product that you can start selling, you begin the sales process. That's how everyone operates.

That is to say, the Trial and Error you're going to go through — when you have a significant number of engineers, you're carrying a hundred thousand dollars a month on your shoulders, and when you make mistakes, every mistake costs a hundred thousand dollars. Not because the mistake itself cost a hundred thousand dollars, but because another month passed, another month, another month, and the money ran out. That's what happens in every company. You build a development team because that's the logical thinking. What am I going to sell if I don't have a product?

Since sales is a complicated thing, very few companies I've met in my life didn't miss what they promised everyone they would sell. You have the Projection you talk about with investors: "First year I'll sell half a million dollars, second year three million, third year ten million. If you build it, they will come. There's no doubt. My genius product will blow everyone away." But almost all of them miss it. And then what happens? The moment the money runs out and you go to raise, they ask you a fair question: "You said you'd sell five million dollars. How much did you sell?" Half a million. "So why should I invest in you? You're not meeting what you said." The money's gone.

When I say companies fail, the same process always happens to them. No company shuts down as long as there's money in the bank, but when the money runs out, they all close. The day the money runs out, you shut the company down. Why? Because nobody is willing to work without a salary, except for the two original founders who keep working for free for a while after that. In many cases, if the company is good, the investors continue to fund it on a "every month I'll give you a check" basis. Meaning, I'm sitting on your vein, watching that you're actually making progress. Not long ago we met a very nice company, and one day the investors said "No, we're not sending a check this month," and that was the end of the story.

How do we reduce the risk? Finally, after an hour and a half, I'm going to tell you something you can actually do something with. The solution is to reverse the order of operations. Instead of developing the product and then trying to sell it, first sell it and then go develop it. Now I know you all think I've lost my mind and you can't sell a product that doesn't exist. You're a million percent right, and in a moment you'll see what you can do. But you need to reverse the order of operations. First start thinking about sales, and then think about development.

The important sentence is: The founders should personally run the trial and error marketing and sales. Remember what I said at the beginning — the goal of a startup is to teach you the profession of being a CEO. Eighty percent of the company's value is in sales. A founder who doesn't get his hands dirty and doesn't deeply understand marketing and sales depends on other people to do the work, and many times he can't even judge whether they're doing a good job or not, because he doesn't know the field. The best thing anyone here with a dream can do is start marketing your idea.

I hope you're sitting down because I'm saying things that really sound like heresy, but they're not. Why? Because at the stage where you're alone or two founders, you have no pressure, no Overhead, no Fixed expenses, no people you're paying salaries to. You're free to do what you need to do. So what do you need to do? You start building and testing your marketing channels, your funnel.

What's a funnel? A funnel is a schematic description of a sales process. At the top of the funnel you have the world's population who have never heard of you — eight billion people who have never heard of you. You want to take those people and bring them down through a funnel. The first stage of the funnel is that they hear about you somehow. The second stage is that they heard about you and it causes them to do something — for example, just click on the link and go to the landing page, open your email. Not read it, God forbid, but open it. Remember, the problem is that we're all busy, we have no time for anything, we have no patience for anything. Getting someone to open your email is a significant achievement.

Question: Doesn't the assumption change depending on how long it takes to bring the product to market? If it'll take me a year to develop the product, what's the point of doing this today when people who already clicked have already forgotten about me? Excellent and very valid question. The goal of what I'm saying is not for you to educate the market right now. The goal is for you to learn how to educate the market. You want to learn: are my customers on TikTok? No. I posted there and nobody responded, but I went on LinkedIn and got tons of responses. I learned something.

Question: And aren't you burning yourself if you get potential customers to click a link that does nothing? Who said it does nothing? Who said anyone is even looking at the product? They first want to understand what this product is supposed to do. You give them a video, you give them text. There's no product. Nobody gets to the product that quickly. If the number of people who responded to me is my market, then I have no market. The people who respond to me are about zero point zero zero one percent of the potential market, because otherwise I'd never grow fast. Yes, it's very possible that I'll disappoint five hundred people out of the five hundred thousand who might be my customers. If I manage to disappoint all of them, then either my marketing was genius and everyone responded, or there's no market.

Always remember what I started with an hour and a half ago: nine out of ten fail. I want to get to where one out of two succeeds. I'm working on percentages. I want to bring you a methodology that dramatically increases your chances of success. That's all I'm doing. I'm not promising you success, but one out of two is better than one out of ten.

You're not burning the market, because the probability that a significant percentage of the market will respond to what you're doing — I wish that upon me and upon you. I would immediately take that and run to investors and say: "Listen, this is unbelievable. I put up an ad and five thousand people clicked on it within twenty-four hours." I wouldn't even need them at all. But that's the rare case. That's Field of Dreams. It happens, but in a dream, and then they write articles about it in newspapers. What you read in the newspaper won't happen to me. Why? Because if I die of a heart attack, nobody will put it as a headline. If a shark eats me, it'll be a headline. Why? Because it doesn't happen. When you see headlines and stories in newspapers, that's the rare, not the common. How many times do you see a headline "Company with fifteen people shut down"? Never. It happens every day. Nobody cares. You always have to remember that — Survivorship Bias.

How do you build the funnel? Let's think at the most simplistic level. You're the founder, you're sitting at home, you have savings from two years of working at Google, and you can afford a year to play around. You say: "I have a genius idea, let's see how I sell it." Let's go to Google and put up some ad, see what happens. Let's go to LinkedIn and do various things. You can start testing your ideas.

Remember, in the early stages of any marketing process, you use only words. You don't do anything other than say a few words. And it's only a few words because nobody's going to read it. If you can't say something that grabs my attention in a sentence and a half, you've lost me. You're all bombarded with noise all day. The first thing I do in the morning is open my email and start Delete, Delete, Delete. I emptied my mailbox. Instead of doing Unsubscribe, I keep them so I can hit Delete because it gives me satisfaction in the morning. But I didn't open a single one of those emails.

Story from the audience: I did a survey through WhatsApp with fifty kids, and then the teacher said bring it to the school, take all four hundred kids. And that's worth gold both in terms of the product and in terms of Product Market Fit. A lot of the things I say, when I say them people go "What, that's obvious. How didn't we do that?" But yes, it's obvious, yet none of us do it. Me neither.

If you look at all these marketing channels, you see that basically it's words. I can write whatever I want, and then either people respond or they don't. I can count. What does "responded" mean? They clicked on the link. When I build a funnel, what interests me is the efficiency of the funnel. How many of the people who were exposed to the ad clicked, took action. Marketing is behavior change that starts with "oops, he clicked the link." That's not trivial. Don't underestimate it. Clicking a link is an enormous mental effort. People have gone to prison for this.

The most critical thing is Call To Action. In everything you want, there needs to be some Call To Action. Why? Because otherwise you can't measure it, and if you can't measure it, you've wasted your time. You want to build a process. You don't actually want to sell. You want to make sure you have a process that works, and it takes a long time to build it. So the Call To Action is your metric. How many people did I manage to move through this chain of that funnel?

And at the end you want to reach some Landing Page. You want to take the person from the ad, bring them to some page you built, and the holy grail is if you manage to get people to sign up, because up until that moment they're anonymous. That's the critical issue. The moment you manage to take someone through the entire process, from the moment they're one of the eight billion who never heard of me, to the moment they sign up and give me their contact information — that's the process you can do without a single bolt of the product. You don't need a single bolt of the product, one leg of the chair, nothing, to go through this entire process. At this stage you already have someone to talk to.

Question: What if in practice I have customers who are already saying okay, I want to buy now, even before I've set out? Where did they come from? I did Customer Validation at conferences. How many conferences do you want to travel around the world to? You need to sell five thousand dollars a day. You need a machine that generates more meetings like that. You have a few customers you met and they were really convinced by you, but that's not a process that will bring your company to profitability.

I'm talking about how to build a profitable company at the lowest possible cost. There's the Lean Startup concept, you all know it. The whole time he's talking about working with validations against customers. Nowhere in the book does he explain where those customers came from. What, my cousin's nephew? Your problem is reaching customers. You want a machine that brings you to customers in growing numbers. That's the goal. And you want to do this not when you have ten or twenty employees, you have to pay them salaries every month, you're under atomic pressure, the money's running out. That's not the stage to think about this.

Question: But what if the number of customers is relatively small and each customer is huge? The time to close a deal is pretty proportional to the size of the deal, unfortunately. If you want to convince someone to buy a yogurt for two shekels, it's easier than convincing someone to buy a yogurt-making machine for two thousand shekels, and that's still easier than convincing someone to spend twenty thousand dollars on a production line. When you move to large deals, your problem is usually not how do I reach customers, because there's a small number of them. I can call all of them on the phone. The sales process is endless. Why? Because suddenly you find out you need to go through IT to make sure you haven't installed viruses on their systems, and after that you need to meet all sorts of regulatory requirements.

At Zoom Info we sold to Bank of America. The first deal was five thousand dollars, closed it on the phone. The second deal too. We ended up reaching a half million dollar deal. It took us three years, and luckily there were intermediate stages along the way that brought us money. It takes a huge amount of time to close deals with big companies, so the problem there is different.

In general, what's common to everything I'm saying is: from the moment you want to start selling to the moment you see money in the bank in growing amounts, there's a very, very long process. Start that process before you have it. I would go to those companies that want to buy from me and start the sales process. Do you have a budget? No, why would I have a budget, there's no product yet. Okay, where do budgets come from? He says budget is once a year, we're in January now, come back in December next year. You've already understood you have a year to wait for a meeting. Start selling. You'll see very quickly what a road of suffering you need to go through, and prepare for it before you've even started the product. You'll find out that a lot of regulatory things you should handle today, not when you're already under pressure.

One or two founders already going through this entire process just to understand the process. And it doesn't matter if you're selling B2C, B2B, million-dollar deals — all of them have long processes. Test them here.

Question: Why don't you show a Cold Outreach channel here? Email Campaign is exactly Outreach — by email, by LinkedIn. Yes, that's exactly what you're saying. I thought you were talking about Cold Calling. How many times when your phone rang and you didn't recognize the person calling did you answer the phone?

Now comes the real clincher. You can do this whole thing for zero money. Meaning a few thousand dollars a month in the worst case, and in the best case a few hundred dollars a month. You can start testing messages and see if you start getting responses. What's worse than the money is the time. Usually what takes time is measuring the response. I put an ad on Google. Google warms up its engines, it doesn't put your ad up immediately. It takes a few days or a week or two, sometimes a month, before it even shows your ad — it tests it first.

Now imagine that during this month you have ten engineers who already finished building the product and are now just collecting salaries. You'll have a heart attack. So do this month while you're sitting with your buddy over a beer. And then you say okay, now let's also test LinkedIn. Now you've placed the ad on Google and you start seeing a click here, a click there. How many of them actually filled out the form and gave you their name? Ah, my landing page isn't convincing anyone. Nobody did registration. Maybe we should put a video there, maybe do a raffle. In short, it takes a huge amount of time until you go step by step and finally manage to get someone who was kind enough to leave their phone number or email and is willing to talk to you. Time, time, time.

Start this while you're still working at another company, in the evenings, on weekends. Don't build me a prototype and proof of concept and all that stuff — it's a waste of your time. You'll raise money much more easily if you come to an investor and show them your funnel and show them how it works. You start from the sales side, you get to much more interesting results than "here, I have a prototype" — very nice, nobody's heard of it.

What do you get if you do this? There are five things that come out of it if you go with the approach of doing an inverse of the operations — first start the marketing and sales process and then build the product.

First of all, you make sure there's even a market. If you're putting up ads and writing content and nobody — or almost nobody — clicks on anything, you'd better know that now, before you've hired ten people and raised a million dollars. That's an alarm bell — something in my assumptions probably isn't working. Maybe I didn't phrase the ad correctly, let's try something else. You have to get results. If there are no results, don't move forward. It's like a yes/no that tells you whether to continue or not.

Second, you'll very quickly discover that some ads work, some audiences respond, some don't — like I described earlier with IntelliChain — we suddenly discovered the entire spare parts market. We hadn't thought about it, but people suddenly came and said, "Yes, this will solve exactly my problem." The moment you start having a dialogue with the market, the people who respond are the ones where you somehow touched on something that interests them, and very often they're not who you thought at all. This gives you the opportunity not just to verify that there's demand, but to understand who the demand is and what message they respond to.

Why is this critical? Because it gives you insight into what I need to focus on in the product. One of the things that happens most in every company is what's called feature creep. "I couldn't sell anything, I'll just add this feature, it'll blow up the world. That didn't work either? No, but I have a genius idea, now we'll do this." That's not going to blow up the world, and the other one won't blow up the world either. It's just hard work. So this prevents you from doing feature creep. You know in advance which things people respond to, which value. You need something that makes people respond to you, and then you know which feature is important to build, because that's the feature people responded to.

The third thing is also critical. All of these things take a lot of time. When you do this in the first stage, you have the ability to improve, and also the ability to start forecasting. When you give a sales forecast, you have some analytical basis of numbers that you know. I placed an ad, it cost me five hundred dollars on Google for the month, I got a thousand clicks, and out of those, a hundred people filled out the form. I at least know where I am in the sales cycle. I would also recommend talking to those people and trying to sell to them — simply by phone or on Zoom — to understand what the chances are that they'll actually buy, not just that they left their phone number. This is important for starting to build a business model based on reality and not on dreams. If you build it, they will not come, trust me.

What happens in the end is that you come out of this with a process that works. You now have enough empirical data that you can say, "I can now hit the road, I can convince investors that the numbers I'm presenting have some basis." Sometimes you don't even need that. You reach a point where you say, "Wow, I've already built the whole thing, I don't even need anyone." Today with Base44 or something like that, now I build it — boom, boom, done. The basic idea here is: start from the sales side, not the other side.

Now we get to the homework. I really ask everyone to do the homework. Go and practice everything I've talked about. We'll send it to you, you don't need to take photos. I suggest doing just two exercises, out of all the big processes. Let's do two exercises just so you get a feel for it.

The first exercise: Google AdWords. When you go to build in Google AdWords, Google asks you a ton of questions, and that's already great for starting to think about them. The first thing it asks is: what are the keywords you want to bid on? There are all kinds of categories. For example, if you're competing with five companies, you can tell Google that every time someone types in the name of my competitor, put my ad up too. You're not allowed to write in the ad "I'm better than X" when you've bid on X — Google doesn't allow that — but you can at least say, "This feature doesn't work with them, with me it does." You're already starting to touch the market. You can start talking about the benefit it brings. If someone is researching longevity, tell them, "My product will extend your life by ten years" — see what happens.

Once someone clicks, they arrive at a landing page. What do you want on the landing page? Somehow make sure there's a call to action — that it's not the last thing they do. You want one more thing to happen. Ideally they'll sign up, but that's hard. You've gotten a person to not just reach the landing page, but to do something. Remember, it's incredibly hard to convince people to do things. If you don't know how, ask your kids — they probably know how to do it.

What else is there? Base44 lets you build some kind of application. You can build a demo for something that doesn't even exist yet. If you get creative, you can take it pretty far, well before there's a product. Go to Nano Banana and build a video of your product. You can be very creative. If you're sitting at home living off your salary from Google, play around. You'll see that you can get very far with these games, and for just a few hundred dollars. Start seeing how this business works.

This is also important because later on you'll need to bring a marketing person into the company, and if you personally have the knowledge of these things, you're already a huge step ahead. Nobody can sell you stories anymore, and that's super critical. Marketing is a complicated subject, and it's very worthwhile for the CEO and the founder to have some understanding from getting their hands dirty with it.

The second thing is LinkedIn. On LinkedIn you have two options. The simple option is to also run an ad, but you can define who you want to see the ad. Unlike Google, where you work with keywords, here you can work with audiences. You say, "I want only VP Sales at companies with sales above ten million dollars." You can define exactly which titles you want to see the ad, in which regions you want it to appear. This forces you to start thinking about who I think could be a potential customer. You can even provide a list of companies, saying, "I want these people at these companies." You can be very, very focused on LinkedIn. Here's a list of five thousand people — I want only them to see my ad.

This will already give you a ton of tools to think about the problem you want to solve and to start getting down to the execution level. Thinking is nice, but once you get your hands dirty, it looks completely different, and very often it's wildly exciting. When you suddenly start getting responses, it's pure adrenaline. So I want you to play around. Like any good homework, there's a due date — Monday, a week and a half from now, January fifth. We won't give feedback, we won't start telling you whether you did it right or wrong, but it does test how serious you are. As you'll recall, after this there's a workshop and after that a residency, and all of these things will be taken into account.

Question: You talked about bringing in the million dollars and going out from there. Once you've brought in the first people, how do you get to the million dollars you're going to raise from a VC, if at all? Once you do what I described here, in my experience, your worldview will be completely different from before you did it. Almost all the entrepreneurs I talk to dedicate about ninety-nine point ninety-nine percent to the product. They're in love with the product, they can tell me every feature they're going to develop. Who will buy it? The whole world, no doubt. I try to shift the entrepreneur's thinking from the great product to how they sell it. After you've done that and started playing, you don't need me anymore. You'll already think completely differently, look at things differently, talk to investors differently, because you'll suddenly see where the value really is and where the problem really is. You need to convince yourself.

Question: I went through these things — the chicken and egg problem. We started with a presentation and then they told us, "Bring five hundred people who sign up first." We did. Then, "Show us the product is valid." We developed it. "Now show us the first five hundred using the product." We got to five hundred. "Now show us fifteen hundred." It's just chicken and egg. Wait — did the users pay money? Not all of them; there are users and there are paying customers. How do you grow the number of paying customers? Keep advertising, or word of mouth, or there's a watermark, there's an automatic first message — I'm B2C. I'm saying: do you know how to build a mechanism that will get you to growing revenue? Activate it.

I promised that I want to get to one out of two, not ninety-eight percent success rate. Life is hard. I just want it not to be ninety percent failure. I can't solve all the world's problems. What you went through with investors is not rare. They're also putting in money; they don't want to risk it. Something in what you're doing probably looks too risky to them. But they're not the only investors. And the question is whether you really need money.

Question: You gave an example that it's important for founders to learn how to market, and that if there's no product, we'd use Base44 to build a POC or MVP. Now, if the founders' team doesn't know how to develop a product and doesn't know how to market, what do they bring to the table? You're a million percent right, but I hope most founders are at least intelligent. To put ads on Google, you only need intelligence. I'm giving you a way — he doesn't know how to develop anything, but at least something he needs to know.

Question: What are the chances of someone like that who doesn't know anything, up against competitors who come to investors and customers and are probably much stronger players than him, if he brings nothing to the table except an idea? You expect me to tell you, "I can take any random idiot and turn him into a genius"? No, I can't. I can take and help a really good entrepreneur who lacks knowledge and who has all kinds of assumptions that I claim are wrong. Taking a person who isn't suited to be an entrepreneur and turning him into a good one — that's something his mother should have done, not me.

I stayed on schedule. Thank you all very much. See you in two weeks.

למה חברות נכשלות וכיצד בונים חברה רווחית

למה חברות נכשלות? אז חברות נכשלות משתי סיבות עיקריות, בעצם משפחות של סיבות. זה לא סיבות בודדות.

אחת, כמו שדיברתי קודם, פשוט מקצוע שאין איפה ללמוד אותו ואז מגיע ה-CEO וצריך בעצם להמציא את הגלגל מחדש. זה מאוד יקר, זה מאוד לא עובד טוב, אז אנחנו רוצים לחסוך את הזמן הזה. לא סתם שמתי דוגמה של residency בבית חולים. לכולם ברור שרופא שסיים שש שנים וגמר בהצטיינות הוא עדיין לא רופא. הוא צריך אחרי זה לעשות התמחות וההתמחות שלו היא בדרך כלל בתת מקצוע מאוד צר. אז אתם מבינים את התהליך. חוץ מ-CEO שאומר יאללה, הוא בוגר שמונה מאתיים, יש לו איזה אלגוריתם פנטסטי, הוא בטח ידע למכור ויביא את החברה להיות גדולה. זה לא נכון. זה פשוט לא נכון.

הסיבה השנייה זה שבעצם אין מתודולוגיה איך בונים חברות. ולא רק שאין מתודולוגיה, יש הרבה מאוד pervasive, מה שאני קורא wrong assumptions, אנחנו נדבר על אחת מהן היום, שפשוט לוקחות את החברות לכיוונים שהם לא בדיוק פרודוקטיביים ומאוד מקטינים את סיכויי ההצלחה שלהם. אז אנחנו מתמודדים עם זה וכמובן אנחנו נותנים הדרכה וכלים איך כן לבנות את הדברים נכון, ואני מקווה שהיום תראו כבר דוגמה אחת ותבינו לאט לאט איך אנחנו עובדים פה.

בשביל לחזור מאיפה מגיעים ה-pervasive assumptions הללו צריך להבין את ה-ecosystem של מי שנותן את הכסף, כי בסוף בעל המאה הוא בעל הדעה, כמו שאנחנו תמיד יודעים. אז כשבא מישהו ומוכן לתת לך כמה מיליוני דולרים, יש לו ציפיות מאוד מאוד ברורות, וזכותו, זה הכסף שלו. אז בואו נראה מה הם צריכים.

קודם כל מה זה VC? VC בעצם זה לא כסף שלהם, הם מגייסים את הכסף מקרנות פנסיה, מחברות ביטוח, מקומות שיש להם כמויות עצומות של מזומנים והן לוקחות חלק קטן ממנו, אומרים נשים אותו בהון סיכון, ואז ה-general partner של זה הוא מה שאנחנו קוראים ה-venture fund, אבל זה בעצם רק המנהלים, זה לא כסף שלהם, והם משקיעים בחברות הסטארט אפ ובסוף הם צריכים להחזיר את הכסף לאותן חברות. זאת אומרת, יש פה מעגל שלם, נתתי לך כסף, תחזיר לי כסף. אל תחזיר לי מניות בחברה, אין לי מה לעשות עם זה. אני חברת ביטוח, אני קרן פנסיה. מה אני אעשה עם מניות? ולכן הכסף צריך לחזור, בשביל שהוא יחזור חייבים שיהיה אקזיט.

עכשיו לוחות הזמנים זה הדבר המעניין כאן. מגייסים את הכסף, בדרך כלל הם מגייסים אותו בשכבות, ככה זה נקרא, וכל שכבה כזו יש לה שבע פלוס שלוש הארכות, שבע שנים, והם יכולים לקבל הארכה שלוש פעמים, סך הכול עשר שנים, שבסוף הם חייבים להחזיר כסף.

מה קורה לפעמים כאשר VC נשאר בסוף תקוע עם שלוש, ארבע, חמש חברות בתוך הפורטפוליו? אז יש חברות VC שקונות את הפורטפוליו שלהם, מסתכלים על כל החבילה ואומרים אוקיי, יש לך את החברות האלה, אתן לך חמישים מיליון דולר, תן לי את כל החברות הללו.

שאלה: דיברת על להביא את המיליון דולר ומשם לצאת החוצה. ברגע שהבאת אנשים ראשונים, איך אתה מגיע למיליון דולר שאתה הולך לגייס מה-VC, אם בכלל? ברגע שאתה עושה את מה שתיארתי פה, מהניסיון שלי, תפיסת העולם שלך תהיה שונה לחלוטין מאשר לפני שעשית את זה. כמעט כל היזמים שאני מדבר איתם מקדישים בערך תשעים ותשע נקודה תשעים ותשע אחוז למוצר. הם מאוהבים במוצר, הם יכולים לספר לי כל feature שהם הולכים לפתח. מי יקנה אותו? כל העולם, אין ספק. אני מנסה להסיט את המחשבה של היזם מהמוצר הנהדר לאיך הוא מוכר אותו. אחרי שעשית את זה והתחלת לשחק, אתה לא צריך אותי יותר. אתה כבר תחשוב אחרת לגמרי, תסתכל על הדברים אחרת, תדבר עם משקיעים אחרת, כי אתה פתאום תראה איפה באמת הערך ואיפה באמת הבעיה. אתה צריך לשכנע את עצמך.

שאלה: אני עברתי את הדברים האלה, ביצת התרנגולת. התחלנו במצגת ואז אמרו לנו "תביאו חמש מאות אנשים ראשונים שיירשמו". הבאנו. אחרי זה "תראו לנו שהמוצר valid". פיתחנו. "עכשיו תראו לנו את החמש מאות הראשונים שמשתמשים במוצר". הגענו לחמש מאות, "תראו לנו עכשיו אלף חמש מאות". זה רק ביצה ותרנגולת. רגע, המשתמשים שילמו כסף? לא כולם, יש משתמשים ויש משלמים. איך אתה מגדיל את מספר המשלמים? ממשיך לפרסם, או מפה לאוזן, או יש watermark, יש הודעה ראשונה אוטומטית — אני B2C. אני אומר: האם אתה יודע לבנות מנגנון שיביא אותך להכנסות שהולכות וגדלות? תפעיל אותו.

אני הבטחתי שאני רוצה להגיע לאחד משניים, לא לתשעים ושמונה אחוזי הצלחה. החיים קשים. אני רק רוצה שזה לא יהיה תשעים אחוז כישלון. אני לא יכול לפתור את כל בעיות העולם. מה שאתה עברת עם המשקיעים הוא לא נדיר. הם גם שמים כסף, הם לא רוצים לסכן אותו. כנראה שמשהו במה שאתה עושה נראה להם מסוכן מדי. אבל הם לא המשקיעים היחידים. והשאלה אם באמת אתה צריך כסף.

שאלה: נתת דוגמה שחשוב שהיזמים ילמדו איך לשווק, ואז שאם אין מוצר נשתמש ב-Base44, נעשה POC או MVP. עכשיו, אם הצוות של ה-founders לא יודע לפתח מוצר ולא יודע לשווק, מה הם מביאים לשולחן? אתה צודק מיליון אחוז, אבל אני מקווה שמרבית ה-founders הם לפחות אינטליגנטים. לשים מודעות בגוגל צריך רק אינטליגנציה. אני נותן לך דרך — הוא לא יודע לפתח כלום, אבל לפחות משהו הוא צריך לדעת.

שאלה: מה הסיכוי של בן אדם כזה שלא יודע כלום מול מתמודדים שמגיעים למשקיעים וללקוחות, ושכנראה הם שחקנים הרבה יותר חזקים ממנו אם הוא לא מביא שום דבר לשולחן חוץ מרעיון? אתה מצפה ממני להגיד לך "אני יכול לקחת כל מטומטם מצוי ולהפוך אותו לגאון"? לא, אני לא יכול. אני יכול לקחת ולעזור ליזם ממש טוב שחסר לו ידע ושיש כל מיני הנחות שהוא צריך לעמוד בהן שאני טוען שהן לא נכונות. לקחת אדם שלא מתאים להיות יזם ולהפוך אותו ליזם טוב — זה אימא שלו הייתה צריכה לעשות, לא אני.

עמדתי בלוחות הזמנים. תודה רבה לכולם. להתראות בעוד שבועיים.

This lecture explores why companies fail and how founders can build profitable ventures by challenging widespread misconceptions about the startup journey. The instructor opens with two fundamental reasons for failure: first, that the CEO role is essentially unlearnable through formal education — unlike medicine, where years of residency follow academic training, founders are expected to succeed with no structured preparation. Second, there is no established methodology for building companies, and the startup ecosystem is riddled with flawed assumptions that lead ventures astray.

To understand where these assumptions originate, the lecture examines the venture capital ecosystem. VCs raise money from pension funds and insurance companies, operating on strict timelines — typically seven years with possible extensions to ten — after which they must return capital. This structure creates intense pressure on startups to reach an exit, whether through an IPO or M&A. The lecture outlines three types of acquisitions: strategic, where a buyer pays above economic value for market positioning or complementary technology; financial, based on profit multiples; and distress sales, which often go unpriced in press releases, suggesting underwhelming outcomes.

A central theme is the staggering complexity of the go-to-market process. Using real company examples, the instructor illustrates how identifying the right customer segment, buyer persona, advertising channel, and pricing model involves solving "equations with a million unknowns." One company, IntelliChain, discovered unexpected demand from importers and spare-parts managers — segments they had never initially targeted — demonstrating that market reality rarely matches initial plans. Building a scalable sales process requires relentless trial and error, continuous measurement, and incremental improvement, all of which take significant time and money.

The lecture challenges the classic startup sequence of raising funds, building a full development team, and only then attempting to sell. Instead, founders are urged to begin marketing experiments early and cheaply, using tools like Google Ads, LinkedIn's audience targeting, landing pages, and no-code platforms to test assumptions before writing a single line of production code. This hands-on approach shifts a founder's mindset from product obsession to genuine understanding of how customers buy, which in turn transforms how they speak to investors and allocate resources.

The session closes with a practical assignment and candid Q&A, reinforcing that while no program can guarantee success, replacing the industry's ninety-percent failure rate with better methodology, earlier market validation, and founder self-education can meaningfully improve the odds.

כדי להבין את מקור ההנחות הללו, יש להכיר את מבנה עולם ההון סיכון. קרנות VC אינן משקיעות כסף עצמי אלא כספים שגויסו מקרנות פנסיה וחברות ביטוח, עם מחויבות להחזיר את ההשקעה תוך מסגרת זמן של כעשר שנים באמצעות אקזיט. לחץ הזמנים הזה מעצב את הציפיות מהחברות ודוחף אותן לצמיחה מהירה ולחיפוש אקזיט אסטרטגי, דבר שבפועל מתרחש לעיתים רחוקות בלבד. תשע מתוך עשר חברות שרודפות אחרי חלום הצמיחה המטאורית נעלמות כשהכסף נגמר.

הטענה המרכזית בהרצאה היא שיזמים משקיעים כמעט את כל מרצם בפיתוח המוצר ומזניחים את שאלת המכירות. הם בונים צוותי פיתוח יקרים, שורפים מאה אלף דולר בחודש, ורק אז מתחילים לגלות שתהליך המכירה מורכב בצורה קיצונית. כדי להמחיש זאת, מוצגות דוגמאות מחברות אמיתיות. חברה אחת שעוסקת בטכנולוגיית וידאו גילתה שקיימים פלחי שוק רבים ושונים, כל אחד מגיב למסרים אחרים, ושיש אינספור נעלמים בנוגע לערוצי השיווק, קהלי היעד ומודל התמחור. חברה אחרת בתחום ניהול מלאי גילתה בהפתעה שלקוחות שלא תכננה לפנות אליהם, כמו יבואנים ומנהלי חלקי חילוף, דווקא הם הנזקקים ביותר למוצר, אך כל אחד מהם דורש שפה שיווקית שונה לחלוטין.

הפתרון המוצע הוא להפוך את הסדר המסורתי ולהתחיל מצד המכירות עוד לפני שיש מוצר מוגמר. באמצעות כלים זולים ונגישים כמו Google AdWords ו-LinkedIn, יזמים יכולים לבדוק הנחות, לזהות קהלי יעד מגיבים ולבנות תובנות אמפיריות. בגוגל עובדים על מילות מפתח ובלינקדאין ניתן למקד קהלים לפי תפקיד, גודל חברה ואזור גיאוגרפי. תהליך הניסוי והטעייה הזה, כשהוא מתבצע לפני גיוס כסף גדול ובניית צוות פיתוח, חוסך משאבים יקרים ומאפשר ליזם להגיע למשקיעים עם נתונים מבוססי מציאות ולא עם חלומות. השורה התחתונה היא ברורה: "If you build it, they will NOT come" — ויזם חכם מתחיל מהשוק, לא מהמוצר.
